questions.q: What is the sum of the three interior angles of any triangle?
questions.a: The sum is always 180 degrees. A wrong answer here suggests the student is confusing this with the properties of a circle (360 degrees) or a square (360 degrees), showing a need to visualize a triangle as half of a rectangle.

questions.q: If a triangle has one angle measuring 95 degrees, can it also be a right-angled triangle? Why?
questions.a: No, it cannot. A right-angled triangle must have one 90-degree angle; if it already has a 95-degree angle, the sum would exceed 180 degrees. Students answering "yes" often fail to realize that a triangle can only have one "special" angle (either obtuse or right) because the sum is strictly limited to 180.

questions.q: A triangle has angles of 50 degrees and 60 degrees. Find the third angle.
questions.a: The third angle is 70 degrees (180 - 50 - 60 = 70). An incorrect answer usually results from poor arithmetic or forgetting the 180-degree rule entirely.

questions.q: Compare an equilateral triangle and a scalene triangle. What is the main difference in their side properties?
questions.a: An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal, while a scalene triangle has all three sides of different lengths. Students often confuse "equilateral" with "isosceles," requiring a review of the prefixes "equi-" (equal) and "iso-" (two).

questions.q: If you have a triangle with sides measuring 5cm, 5cm, and 8cm, how would you classify it and why?
questions.a: It is an isosceles triangle because exactly two sides are equal in length. If a student calls it scalene, they have miscounted the sides; if they call it equilateral, they have ignored the 8cm measurement.

questions.q: Draw a triangle that is both obtuse and isosceles. What would be the minimum requirements for the sides and angles?
questions.a: The triangle must have two equal sides and one angle greater than 90 degrees. A poor answer ignores the "isosceles" requirement (two sides equal) or draws an acute triangle instead, showing a lack of synthesis between the two classification types.
